p.t: From the Village to the City
p.x:
Two years ago, my family moved from a small village to Bangkok. Our old house was on a hill, and there were rice fields everywhere. Life in the village was quiet and relaxed. We breathed fresh air every day.
Bangkok is very big and lively. There are tall buildings, big shopping malls and lots of people. At first, I didn't like it. It was noisy, and I missed my friends.
Now I like the city more. There are many things to do. But sometimes I think the city is too busy, and I miss the green hills. My little brother says the village was dull because there was no cinema. I think both places are good in different ways.

More and more Thai people are moving from the countryside to cities. Why? The main reason is opportunity: there are more jobs, universities and hospitals in big cities. People also enjoy the convenience of city life: you can buy almost anything, at any time, and the nightlife is exciting, especially downtown.
However, city life has disadvantages. The cost of living is high, and many people live in small flats on the outskirts and spend hours in traffic. The pace of life is fast-paced and stressful, and there is little greenery. Overcrowding can also be a problem.
The countryside, by contrast, is peaceful. Villages are often tight-knit communities where everyone knows each other. But some villages are isolated, far from hospitals and good schools, and public services are limited.
Today, things are changing. With fast broadband, some people now work online from the countryside. Others choose a suburban home in an area that is well-connected to the city by train. Some companies even relocate their offices to smaller cities. Migration is no longer only in one direction.

For most of human history, the majority of people lived in rural areas. That changed around 2007, when, for the first time, more people lived in cities than in the countryside. Urbanisation has transformed economies, creating unprecedented wealth, but it has also produced a growing divide between thriving cities and declining rural regions.
In many countries, the result has been a steady exodus of young people from villages. Attracted by education and careers, the most talented and ambitious often leave and rarely return, a form of brain drain that leaves rural areas with ageing populations. Some villages in Japan, South Korea and parts of Europe now face severe depopulation, with schools closing and houses abandoned. Meanwhile, the hustle and bustle of the city brings its own problems, from pollution to loneliness.
Governments have tried various solutions. Some have attempted to decentralise, moving government offices and universities to provincial towns. Others offer grants to families who move to rural areas, or invest in infrastructure to make villages more attractive. Remote working, which grew rapidly during the pandemic, has allowed some professionals to combine city salaries with a tranquil rural lifestyle, and some have helped revitalise struggling communities.
Yet the picture of an idyllic countryside can be misleading. Rural life may offer beauty and community, but it can also mean limited healthcare, fewer job opportunities and long journeys. Similarly, many people settle in the commuter belt, hoping to enjoy the best of both worlds, only to spend hours travelling each day. The ideal balance, it seems, depends on each person's priorities.
